items.title: INFLUENCE OF INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGY (ICT) ON COGNITIVE ENGAGEMENT AMONG SENIOR SECONDARY SCHOOL STUDENTS IN MINNA METROPOLIS, NIGER STATE, NIGERIA
items.abstract: This study examined influence of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) on cognitive engagement among senior secondary school students in Minna Metropolis, Niger State, Nigeria. Two objectives guided the study, and two research questions were raised and answered. Two null hypotheses were formulated and tested at 0.05 levels of significance. Descriptive survey design was adopted for the study. The population of the study comprised of 3,023 senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State. The sample of the study was 311 senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State which was selected through multi-stage sampling procedure. Influence of Information and Communication Technology on Students’ Cognitive Engagement Questionnaire’ (IICTSCEQ) was used for data collection and it was validated by three experts from the Department of Counselling Psychology, IBBU Lapai. Test re-test method was used to obtain the reliability coefficient and co-efficient-value was 0.82. The data collected were analyzed through the use of Statistical Product for Service Solution (SPSS- version 24). Frequency counts and percentage were used to present the demographic information of the respondents, mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions, simple linear regression was used to test hypotheses 1 and independent sample t-test was used to test hypotheses 2 at 0.05 levels of significance. The findings of the study revealed among others that ICT has a significant positive influence on cognitive engagement of senior secondary school students in Minna Metropolis Niger State; and there is no significant difference between male and female respondents in the influence of ICT on cognitive engagement among senior secondary school students in Minna Metropolis, Niger State. The study concluded that ICT significantly influences the cognitive engagement of senior secondary school students by improving critical thinking to learning. Based on these findings, the researcher recommended that Teachers should combine ICT tools with innovative teaching strategies that promote critical thinking and problem-solving skills to enhance the cognitive engagement of senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State, Nigeria; and School administrators and teachers should ensure that ICT instructional strategies are designed to equally stimulate the cognitive engagement of both male and female senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State, Nigeria.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial generativa y autorregulación del aprendizaje en la educación superior ecuatoriana: Una revisión sistemática
items.abstract: The objective of this study was to synthesize evidence regarding the relationship between the academic use of generative artificial intelligence and self-regulated learning among higher education students in Ecuador. A systematic literature review was conducted, involving a structured web-based search for publications in Spanish and English from the 2023–2026 period. Out of 25 identified records, five publications were selected. The selection process was documented using a diagram adapted from the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and methodological quality was assessed using the MMAT 2018 instrument. The narrative synthesis revealed positive associations between the frequency of generative artificial intelligence use and both learning planning and monitoring. One intervention, which combined three artificial intelligence tools with pedagogical guidance, showed an increase in scores for goal setting and self-monitoring. Self-evaluation was addressed by only a single specific estimate, derived from a study that contained discrepancies in its reported sample size. It was concluded that, among the publications examined, the evidence was more consistent for planning and monitoring than for self-evaluation. Variations in research designs and instruments limited the ability to establish causal links or generalize the findings to the context of higher education in Ecuador.

items.title: INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL NA EDUCAÇÃO E OS IMPACTOS DO USO DE FERRAMENTAS DIGITAIS NO PROCESSO DE APRENDIZAGEM
items.abstract: The transformations resulting from the spread of artificial intelligence in educational environments have opened up new perspectives for the organization of teaching, while simultaneously raising questions about its impact on knowledge construction and students' intellectual autonomy. Given this context, the research aimed to analyze the effects of artificial intelligence and digital tools on learning processes, examining their pedagogical potential, operational limitations, and ethical and social implications. To this end, a qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive study was conducted, based on a literature review of scientific works published in Portuguese between 2019 and 2026, sourced from the SciELO, DOAJ, and Google Scholar databases. The analysis of the literature revealed opportunities for methodological diversification, the personalization of educational experiences, and the enhancement of teaching activities through the use of intelligent systems. Conversely, challenges were identified, including inequalities in access, a lack of digital literacy, algorithmic biases, and risks to authorship and critical thinking. The findings indicate that the integration of technology does not, in itself, guarantee improvements in the quality of learning, as its effects depend on the pedagogical and institutional conditions under which it is implemented. It is therefore concluded that the use of artificial intelligence in education requires qualified pedagogical mediation, human oversight, ethical guidelines, and strategies that preserve the student's role as an active agent—ensuring a convergence between technological innovation and the development of cognitive, reflective, and social competencies.

items.title: Intent Representation and Human Distraction Modulate the Effects of Legible Robot Motion in Hallway Navigation
items.abstract: Legibility in human-robot interaction (HRI) is often described as the property of robot motion that enables an observer to confidently and quickly infer the robot’s intent. Mature frameworks exist for generating legible motion in front of static observers, typically by making the robot’s destination apparent as early as possible. Social robot navigation in public spaces, however, presents a different challenge: pedestrians are themselves in motion, often with divided attention, and must coordinate with the robot in real time. In such encounters, where the robot is ultimately headed may matter less to a pedestrian than how it intends to pass them. This raises two questions: which aspect of intent should legible motion convey, and does legibility remain beneficial when pedestrians are not fully attentive to the robot? We address these questions in the ubiquitous and demanding scenario of hallway navigation, through two controlled user studies comparing multiple legibility formulations implemented within a shared model predictive control framework. Study 1 (N = 45) compares destination-based and passing-side intent representations, showing that the latter, particularly when adaptively updated, allows for smoother human motion and is perceived as more competent and less mentally and physically demanding than the former. Study 2 (N = 45) examines the effect of pedestrian attention, demonstrating that legible motion supports smooth human motion even under distraction, although this benefit is not consistently reflected in subjective ratings. Together, these findings suggest that effective legible motion in social robot navigation benefits from interaction-level intent representations that support coordination, with some effects persisting even when human attention is divided. Code is available at https://github.com/fluentrobotics/Legible_MPPI and footage from our experiments at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P5O5BwfcUCo.

items.title: Jane Austen's Fiction as an Anticipatory Critique of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: In twenty-first-century discourse, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly framed as a system that reduces human behaviour, sentiment, and relationship to pattern recognition, predictive modelling, and data optimization. While this phenomenon is historically unprecedented in its technological architecture, its underlying socio-behavioural mechanics- reducing human subjectivity to structural metrics and formulaic calculations- are far from new. This paper positions the Regency novels of Jane Austen as an anticipatory critique of the algorithmic reduction of human interiority. Operating during the onset of the Industrial Revolution and the rise of early capitalist market logic, Austen observed a societal impulse to treat human relationships as transactional math. By closely reading Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility, and Emma, this paper explores how Austen's "calculating characters" function as early analogues to predictive algorithms and large language models, showing that her ultimate defense of the "uncalculating" mind serves as a vital framework for preserving human agency against automated optimization.

items.title: Leadership Skills in AI-Driven Organizations: Cultivating Resilience, Adaptability, and Foresight for Leaders Managing AI-Enabled Teams
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across industries is fundamentally transforming organizational structures, decision-making processes, workforce dynamics, and leadership practices. As intelligent systems increasingly automate routine tasks and augment human capabilities, leaders face new challenges related to strategy, workforce development, ethics, organizational transformation, and innovation management. Traditional leadership approaches, while still valuable, are often insufficient for navigating the complexities of AI-driven environments characterized by rapid technological change, uncertainty, and continuous disruption. This article explores the emerging competencies required for leadership in AI-enabled organizations, focusing on resilience, adaptability, strategic foresight, digital literacy, ethical stewardship, and human-centered innovation. Drawing upon contemporary research and global examples, the article examines how organizations can cultivate leadership capabilities that balance technological advancement with organizational sustainability, employee well-being, and long-term value creation. It argues that successful AI leadership is not merely about managing technology but about leading people through technological transformation.

items.title: Legal Liability for Harm Caused by Artificial Intelligence and Algorithms: A Comparative Study of Criminal, Civil, and Administrative Liability in the European Union and the United Arab Emirates
items.abstract: This research examines the topic of “Legal Liability for Harm Caused by Artificial Intelligence and Algorithms: A Comparative Study of Criminal, Civil, and Administrative Liability in the European Union and the United Arab Emirates.” It aims to explain the legal framework governing the use and processing of data and information, and to identify the harm that may result from algorithmic outputs, particularly violations of privacy, damage to reputation, the spread of misleading information, fraud, identity theft, and the unlawful disclosure of personal data. The research uses a descriptive, analytical, and comparative approach. It describes and analyses relevant legal provisions and compares the legal protection measures, oversight mechanisms, and penalties in the European Union and the United Arab Emirates. The study also examines civil liability, including its main elements and the conditions for compensation for material and non-material damage. It addresses administrative liability in terms of regulatory obligations, supervision, and penalties. In addition, it examines criminal liability, including the elements of a crime and the attribution of criminal acts to natural or legal persons, depending on the nature of the act. The findings show that the involvement of multiple parties in developing, operating, and using artificial intelligence systems makes liability more complex. The mere fact that harm results from an algorithmic output is not sufficient to establish liability. It is necessary to determine whether an unlawful act occurred, whether damage was caused, whether there is a causal link between the act and the damage, and whether the legally required criminal intent exists. The study recommends updating legislation governing liability for harm caused by artificial intelligence, strengthening transparency and human oversight, improving the preservation of digital evidence and the proof of causation, clarifying the obligations of developers, providers, and users, and enhancing cooperation between regulatory and judicial authorities. These measures would help protect rights and achieve a balance between technological innovation and legal accountability.

items.title: LITMUS - Literature Informed Testbed for Mapping Usecases and Synthesizing Risk-Cards
items.abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in real-world applications has heightened the need for systematic, safety-oriented deployment frameworks. Existing approaches typically prioritize the construction of datasets and risk cards around the LLM and AI architecture itself, yet they provide scant consideration for the specific use-case that drives model selection. This omission is problematic because any practical AI deployment begins with a detailed use-case description that informs the assessment of contextual hazards. In this paper, we introduce a structured pipeline that, given a use-case, automatically produces a tailored dataset and an accompanying risk card. The process ensures that identified risks are tightly coupled to the use-case, and it offers traceable evidence from peer-reviewed literature to substantiate each risk to use-case relationship. Prior claim-verification methods (FActScore, FactReasoner) have been validated for factual claims. Risk-relevance is a hypothetical claim about possible harm, and whether evidence retrieval can meaningfully assess such claims remains untested. Literature-Informed Testbed for Mapping Use-cases and Synthesizing (LITMUS) risk cards are the first systematic attempt to characterize this adaptation. We evaluated the pipeline using the MIT Risk Taxonomy and achieved a 0.91 F1-score with a list of 320 samples from the benchmark risk dataset that was considered. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating robust, evidence-based risk assessments for LLM deployments.

items.title: Measuring Empowerment at the Workplace With Total Worker Health ® ‐Aligned Instruments
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The Total Worker Health® (TWH) approach has broadened the factors recognized as contributing to worker health, safety, and well-being. Many work conditions attended to by the TWH approach, however, are shaped by power relations between workers and employers, and are reinforced by regulation and social, economic, and political norms. Recognizing that concepts of power and power relations can be a difficult topic for occupational health and safety professionals and researchers to discuss, this paper introduces the concepts of structural and psychological empowerment, and, after describing validated tools used to measure these concepts, assesses the extent to which these concepts are captured in survey instruments used in TWH research. METHODS: This study uses a narrative literature review to identify validated instruments used to measure structural and psychological empowerment. The concepts and instruments are then compared to items in the NIOSH WellBQ survey, the Healthy Work Survey, and the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire III. RESULTS: The NIOSH WellBQ, Healthy Work Survey, and Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire III each capture some elements of structural and psychological empowerment, but require supplemental questions to capture all elements of these concepts. CONCLUSIONS: Occupational health and safety professionals and researchers must become more comfortable talking about power and power relations because changing these workplace characteristics may improve worker health, safety, and well-being through many elements of the TWH approach.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

items.title: META-SKILLS AS AN INTEGRATIVE FRAMEWORK FOR HUMAN DEVELOPMENT IN THE CONTEXT OF INTERACTION WITH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
items.abstract: The article provides a theoretical rationale for the need to develop meta-skills as a regulatory level of human personal, educational and professional capability amid the spread of digital technologies and generative artificial intelligence.The aim of the study is to clarify the meaning of the concept of "meta-skills", identify the factors that necessitate their development, and construct a structural and functional model of meta-skills for a hybrid digital and mental environment.The methods of theoretical analysis, comparative analysis of international competence frameworks, conceptual synthesis and modelling were applied.Meta-skills are proposed to be understood as an integrated higher-order capacity that enables the conscious acquisition, regulation, verification, transfer and ethically responsible application of technical and professional skills and social and communication skills in new contexts.Six interrelated components are identified: metacognitive and learning, critical and informational, self-regulatory, adaptive and transfer, social and communicative, and digital and ethical.It is substantiated that the system's fundamental mechanism is the capacity for lifelong learning, while its effectiveness is manifested in the preservation of human agency, the ability to verify AI-generated results, manage attention and emotional load, transfer ways of acting across situations, and take responsibility for making the final decision.Principles for developing meta-skills and criteria for assessing them are identified that are suitable for designing educational and professional programmes.The practical significance of the findings lies in the possibility of incorporating the proposed cycle into the training of specialists in various fields.

items.title: Model choice and prompt framing in LLM sustainability judgments
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for sustainability assessment and decision support, yet their judgments may depend on the selected model and on how the task is defined. We compare 13 locally executed open-weight LLMs on 80 author-written sustainability scenarios using three prompt families that ask which actor should be responsible, bear the costs, or initiate action. Each model answered at two temperature settings with 100 repetitions, producing 624,000 deposited outputs, of which 610,708 contain a complete score vector. Scores were analyzed as relative actor support after removing each response’s overall level. Within this instrument, the cost prompt family produced the highest cross-model disagreement, exceeding both responsibility and catalyst by 7.37 points (question-cluster 95% intervals 5.56−9.15 and 5.38−9.36, describing variation across these 80 scenarios). It also produced the most lead-actor disagreement and the lowest full consensus. Moving from catalyst to cost reduced relative support for government and increased it for individuals and firms; moving from cost to responsibility largely reversed this pattern. These differences exceeded temperature-setting differences and persisted under model exclusion, alternative score transformations and tie rules, missing-response checks, and stems without explicit cost wording. Exploratory category patterns are conditional on uneven item coverage. Secondary rationale-language comparisons show the same within-model ordering but not the most cross-model variation under cost. Operational use should disclose model, prompt, and temperature choices; compare plausible alternatives; repeat generations; and refer high-disagreement judgments for human deliberation.

items.title: Operational Assurance for LLM-Based Systems under Governance Opacity
items.abstract: In the contemporary artificial intelligence ecosystem, foundation models are increasingly deployed under AI-as-a-Service (AIaaS) schemes characterized by high technical opacity, technological concentration, and limited external auditing capability over governance, training, and internal operational processes. Under these conditions, traditional ethical oversight approaches that focus exclusively on corporate governance or on internal model inspection become insufficient to ensure effective control over AI systems deployed in real-world contexts. This work proposes a pragmatic operational assurance framework inspired by Zero-Trust principles from cybersecurity, which shifts effective auditing efforts toward the application layer, where risk acquires observable, contextualized, and operationally verifiable properties. The proposal articulates two complementary evaluation levels: a black-box evaluation aimed at characterizing general behaviors, vulnerabilities, and risky capabilities of foundation models through conversational scanning, and a grey-box evaluation focused on the operational contextualization of risk within the actual deployment environment of the audited application. The framework incorporates mechanisms to move from general, CVSS-inspired severity metrics toward contextualized operational risk assessments that take into account user profiles, industrial domains, and organizational knowledge. In addition, the proposal strengthens practical auditability through digitally signed explainability reports (signed XAI reports), designed to support verifiable traceability, continuous monitoring, and operational accountability in LLM-based sociotechnical systems.

items.title: PatchLens: Adapting Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques for Non-Expert Audiences
items.abstract: A chat interface presents a reply as finished text, concealing a model that predicts at every position and reruns. Mechanistic interpretability can show how a large language model produces text, but its tools are built for researchers. We present PatchLens, a browser interface that runs logit lens and activation patching on remotely served research-scale models. Each layer's state appears as the tokens it comes closest to, laid out by layer and input position; an intervention is a drag from one cell onto another. The tokens a learner reads are the tokens they manipulate. In a between-subjects study with 61 non-experts, the comparison against Transformer Explainer was inconclusive on post-test knowledge. PatchLens participants wrote their own prompts (21 of 32 against 1 of 29), reported lower mental demand, and located their difficulty in the interface rather than the material. We read the null as evidence about what such an instrument measures.

items.title: Pengaruh Bias Kognitif Terhadap Ketepatan Pengambilan Keputusan Keuangan Manajerial Mahasiswa Akuntansi Universitas Nias
items.abstract: Mahasiswa Akuntansi Universitas Nias sebagai calon tenaga profesional di bidang akuntansi dan keuangan perlu memiliki kemampuan mengambil keputusan keuangan secara rasional dan tepat. Namun, dalam proses pengambilan keputusan, individu tidak selalu bertindak sepenuhnya berdasarkan informasi objektif. Bias kognitif, seperti anchoring bias, overconfidence bias, dan confirmation bias, dapat memengaruhi cara seseorang menerima, mengolah, dan menilai informasi keuangan. Studi ini bertujuan mengetahui sejauh mana tiga jenis bias kognitif, yakni anchoring bias, overconfidence bias, dan confirmation bias, memengaruhi ketepatan keputusan keuangan manajerial mahasiswa Akuntansi Universitas Nias. Pendekatan yang dipakai adalah kuantitatif asosiatif. Data primer dihimpun melalui kuesioner skala Likert lima poin yang memuat 30 butir pernyataan berbasis empat skenario kasus keuangan manajerial, dan diisi oleh 35 mahasiswa yang dipilih dengan teknik purposive sampling. Data dianalisis menggunakan statistik deskriptif, uji kualitas instrumen, uji asumsi klasik, dan regresi linear berganda. Hasil menunjukkan anchoring bias memiliki koefisien positif tetapi tidak signifikan terhadap ketepatan keputusan (B = 0,450; p = 0,055), sedangkan overconfidence bias (B = −0,272; p = 0,447) dan confirmation bias (B = 0,066; p = 0,770) juga tidak berpengaruh signifikan. Secara simultan, ketiga bias tersebut tidak berpengaruh signifikan terhadap ketepatan keputusan (F = 1,926; p = 0,146) dengan R² sebesar 0,157. Kesimpulan dari penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa variasi ketepatan keputusan dalam sampel lebih banyak berkaitan dengan faktor lain di luar model.

items.abstract: The growing accessibility of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has expanded opportunities for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to automate routine cognitive work and support managerial decisions. This article examines the potential influence of GenAI use on operational efficiency and decision-making quality through a directed integrative literature review. Eight core sources comprising peer-reviewed studies and international institutional reports published between 2023 and 2026 were analyzed using thematic synthesis. The analysis identifies three major mechanisms: faster content and information processing, broader generation of business alternatives, and improved knowledge accessibility for resource-constrained firms. Evidence from professional writing and customer-service settings indicates productivity gains under specific task conditions, while OECD survey results suggest self-reported benefits among GenAI-using SMEs. However, findings from large organizations and selected countries cannot be generalized automatically to Indonesian MSMEs. The quality of managerial decisions still depends on data accuracy, human verification, workers’ digital skills, and privacy safeguards. A practical implementation framework is proposed to connect low-risk pilots, performance indicators, and accountable human oversight. The article concludes that GenAI should be treated as a complementary decision-support capability rather than a substitute for managerial judgment.

items.title: Principles and Applications of Computerised Process Instrumentation and Control Systems to Advance Industrial Process Operations in Nigeria
items.abstract: Nigerian industrial revolution has progressed through stages of development in different periods (eras). The requirement for operator interface in the distributed control system was fulfilled by Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA). Operator station enabled information systems automation to enhance enterprise resource Integration which enables better strategization to overcome profit squeeze and liquidation. The Programmable Logic Controller provided solution to sequence automation and fast reaction systems where scan times, sequences and event recording are required. Since 1971, the distributed control system has undergone progressive advancement, some of which include: Integration of Microprocessor, Human-Machine interface, Networked Systems, Modular design, integration with Enterprise Resource Planning along with manufacturing execution systems and Internet of Things (IoTs) which enables adoption of industrial procedures: Data Analytics, Cloud Computing, Edge Computing and Cyber- security Protection. Integration of Digital Twins, Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence will make Distributed Control Systems smarter, more efficient and adaptable with many benefits. In Nigeria, the integration of advanced technologies such as Artificial Intelligence into the Distributed Control Systems will enhance efficiency, greater productivity and higher product quality resulting in reduced costs and increased profits. The Nigerian Government is therefore encouraged to overcome the challenges and fully implement artificial intelligence in Nigeria.

items.title: Redesigning Educational System: Evaluating the Importance of Educational Certificates Versus Work Experiences in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Rapid technological change raises an urgent question for higher education: how can universities prepare students for workplaces that may change substantially before they graduate? During several years of study, professional tools and expectations can develop faster than curricula are updated, leaving graduates to acquire essential practical skills after entering employment. The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) makes this challenge more pressing. Online courses and self-directed learning also raise questions about the value of investing in a university qualification when alternative routes offer more immediate professional training. If universities cannot demonstrate how their programmes support professional capability, they risk weakening their appeal to prospective students. This study examines the perceived gap between university preparation and workplace requirements, exploring how participants understand the contribution of educational credentials and practical experience to their professional development. It draws on 35 personal, semi-structured interviews with purposively selected participants from diverse professional and educational backgrounds. Interview material was analysed using reflexive thematic analysis supported by MAXQDA, with curriculum preferences reported separately as descriptive counts. Participants described acquiring changing technologies through work and continued learning. Their responses distinguished the value of qualifications in opening opportunities from the practical capability needed to perform effectively. AI supported faster production, but its use required independent judgement and verification. Universities need to make the practical value of higher education visible throughout students’ learning, while developing the capacity to keep learning as workplace demands change.

items.title: Rehearse Before You Travel: A Conceptual Model of AI-Assisted Travel Rehearsal and the Self-Fading AI Hypothesis
items.abstract: Tourists abroad routinely face short, consequential service encounters: an inflated taxi fare, a pharmacy visit in an unfamiliar language, a room that does not match the booking. Research on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in tourism has concentrated on how such systems help travellers plan, choose and delegate decisions, and on how AI support during a trip shapes confidence and satisfaction. Separately, research in language education, health-professions education and workplace training shows that rehearsal with simulated counterparts can build skills, although transfer of those skills to real settings is conditional rather than automatic. This conceptual article brings these streams together for the tourist. It proposes the AI-Assisted Travel Rehearsal (ATR) model, an iterative cycle in which travellers rehearse anticipated encounters with general-purpose conversational AI before and during a trip, receive minimal AI support in real encounters, and reflect on each encounter to plan the next rehearsal. Drawing on social cognitive theory, experiential learning theory, the transactional model of stress and coping, scaffolding and fading, and transfer-of-training research, the article specifies a mechanism linking rehearsal to mastery experience, situational self-efficacy and behavioural capability, conditional transfer, and progressive AI fading. Its central claim, the Self-Fading AI Hypothesis, holds that well-designed AI support should reduce travellers' reliance on AI in real encounters without loss of independent performance; reduced AI use alone is not treated as evidence of autonomy. The article states six propositions with explicit conditions of support, identifies which can be tested confirmatorily, and proposes a randomised, actively controlled classroom experiment with AI-unavailable and AI-available transfer tasks, followed by a multilevel field study of first-time international travellers. No empirical results are reported.

items.title: Rehearse Before You Travel: A Conceptual Model of AI-Assisted Travel Rehearsal and the Self-Fading AI Hypothesis
items.abstract: Tourists abroad routinely face short, consequential service encounters: an inflated taxi fare, a pharmacy visit in an unfamiliar language, a room that does not match the booking. Research on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in tourism has concentrated on how such systems help travellers plan, choose and delegate decisions, and on how AI support during a trip shapes confidence and satisfaction. Separately, research in language education, health-professions education and workplace training shows that rehearsal with simulated counterparts can build skills, although transfer of those skills to real settings is conditional rather than automatic. This conceptual article brings these streams together for the tourist. It proposes the AI-Assisted Travel Rehearsal (ATR) model, an iterative cycle in which travellers rehearse anticipated encounters with general-purpose conversational AI before and during a trip, receive minimal AI support in real encounters, and reflect on each encounter to plan the next rehearsal. Drawing on social cognitive theory, experiential learning theory, the transactional model of stress and coping, scaffolding and fading, and transfer-of-training research, the article specifies a mechanism linking rehearsal to mastery experience, situational self-efficacy and behavioural capability, conditional transfer, and progressive AI fading. Its central claim, the Self-Fading AI Hypothesis, holds that well-designed AI support should reduce travellers' reliance on AI in real encounters without loss of independent performance; reduced AI use alone is not treated as evidence of autonomy. The article states six propositions with explicit conditions of support, identifies which can be tested confirmatorily, and proposes a randomised, actively controlled classroom experiment with AI-unavailable and AI-available transfer tasks, followed by a multilevel field study of first-time international travellers. No empirical results are reported.

items.title: Revisión del uso de la IA en los procesos de planificación en la gerencia de proyectos
items.abstract: The inherent complexity and exposure of projects to disruptive events during the formulation, planning, and execution stages necessitate the adoption of technological tools that optimize the processes underlying these stages and, consequently, support decision-making. In this context, this research project aims to identify opportunities for applying AI to key project planning activities. To this end, a literature review was conducted using both qualitative and quantitative evidence, resulting in the selection and analysis of 51 academic articles. Similarly, the PMI, ISO 21502, IPMA, and PRINCE2 standards were examined to generate a unified framework for the main planning activities. The results revealed AI applications in semantic analysis, predictive analytics, optimization algorithms, automation, and workflow integration. Technologies such as language models, generative artificial intelligence, machine learning, reinforcement learning, and AI agents were also analyzed. These technologies enabled the reduction of repetitive tasks, improved accuracy in deviation detection, and thus optimized project planning. It was demonstrated that AI can strengthen and enhance the performance of key project planning activities.

items.title: Social Media Use Intensity and Academic Procrastination among Construction Vocational Students: Duration Dominance and Implications for Productive Time Management
items.abstract: Productive task time is a core concern of human-performance and work-system design, and construction vocational students are forming the time-use habits they will bring into the workforce. This study examined how social media use intensity, and its attention, absorption, duration, and frequency facets, is associated with academic procrastination among 117 randomly selected eleventh-grade Building Modeling and Information Design (DPIB) students at a public vocational high school in Bandung, Indonesia. Confirmatory factor analysis showed that reverse-keyed items loaded near zero on their constructs; the retained items had composite reliabilities of .74–.89 and discriminant validity (HTMT < .85). Intensity was high (67.59%) and procrastination moderate (54.78%). Intensity was positively associated with procrastination (β = .444, 95% CI for B [0.189, 0.415], R² = .197), and the association held with CFA-refined scales (β = .409) and after excluding influential cases. Duration dominated the facets, accounting for 63.5% of the explained variance (bootstrap 95% CI 44.1–74.0%), whereas attention, absorption, and frequency added no significant unique prediction. A sensitivity analysis indicated that an unmeasured confounder would need correlations of at least .565 with both variables to overturn the inference. Because the design is cross-sectional, the results indicate association rather than causation. They support measurable time-allocation interventions: device-free work blocks, milestone-based project scheduling, and self-regulation guidance.

items.title: Speaking From the Self: How State Authenticity Increases Subjective Agency and Challenging Voice
items.abstract: People often avoid speaking up not because they lack ideas, but because voice feels socially risky. We examine whether and how state authenticity-the feeling of alignment with one's true self-influences challenging voice. Across five experimental studies (four preregistered) spanning field and laboratory samples (N = 2,195), we manipulate state authenticity and test its relationship with challenging voice. Findings suggest that state authenticity can facilitate challenging voice, with effects emerging either directly or indirectly through increased subjective agency. The agency pathway remained evident when self-presentational concern was modeled simultaneously (Study 3b) and was stronger among individuals lower in extraversion, higher in agreeableness, and higher in dispositional authenticity (Study 4). Drawing on self-determination and self-transcendence perspectives, we argue that authentic states can shift regulation toward internally endorsed action, helping individuals act on their convictions despite interpersonal risk. These findings clarify how and for whom authenticity translates into challenging interpersonal communication.

items.title: Standoff Explosive Detection by Hyperspectral Imaging: A Requirements-Based Review
items.abstract: Standoff optical detection of explosives must meet multiple operational requirements simultaneously. This review formalizes seven quantitative operational requirements, derived from blast safety doctrine, forensic contamination data, published standards, and detection theory, each evaluated using an explicit scoring criterion: standoff distance, trace sensitivity, false alarm rate, acquisition speed, selectivity, environmental operating envelope, and moving-target capability. Guided by PRISMA 2020, the review evaluates the 2020–2026 literature on hyperspectral imaging (HSI) together with four active spectroscopies as a comparative baseline: Raman, terahertz, laser-induced breakdown, and laser-induced fluorescence. Assessed against this requirements-based framework, none of the active spectroscopies satisfies all seven requirements, reflecting predominantly point-wise, laboratory-bound architectures. HSI provides the imaging architecture largely absent from these techniques, but neither the passive nor the active branch satisfies all seven requirements. Passive HSI provides standoff imaging from weak overtone bands but no demonstrated trace sensitivity, whereas active HSI accesses the fundamental long-wave infrared fingerprint bands and reports tested or estimated trace-level loadings only over a few metres, without an established detection limit. Standoff distance and sensitivity are rarely measured together, limiting assessment of operational performance. Deployment is constrained not only by sensing physics but also by the lack of standardized performance evidence, public benchmark datasets, and operational validation.

items.title: Template-guided large language model workflows improve usability but not time and effectiveness for building energy modelling
items.abstract: Although building energy modelling (BEM) effectively identifies sources of energy waste, it is a time-consuming, manual, and costly solution. Generative AI, specifically large language models (LLMs), could expedite BEM, but studies have not extensively validated the technology with users. Our study compares effectiveness, time, and usability for 13 non-experts modelling a complex BEM task using both traditional and template-guided LLM workflows. We analyse participants' models, survey responses, and screen activity. For effectiveness, the template-guided workflow results in fewer failed tasks but no significant gains in accuracy. For time, the traditional method is faster for three out of five modelling stages, with one reaching statistical significance. For usability, users overall prefer the template-guided workflow and rate it higher in satisfaction, perceived accuracy, and learnability, especially for more open-ended tasks. These findings indicate that generative AI could improve BEM usability and thereby ultimately enhance access and adoption of building energy modelling.

items.title: The 2025 Google Code Golf Championship
items.abstract: For over half a decade, the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus has played a critical role in evaluating the fluid intelligence and skill acquisition efficiency of machine learning systems. While the dataset has proven especially useful in advancing program synthesis, few investments have been made in distilling the transformational logic of these tasks into their most irreducible computational forms. In conjunction with the NeurIPS 2025 Competition Track, we organized the 2025 Google Code Golf Championship, a three-month online challenge designed to elicit minimal Python solutions for all training puzzles in the seminal ARC-AGI-1 benchmark suite. Sponsored by Google DeepMind and funded with $100,000 in prizes, the contest attracted over 1,000 teams and yielded tens of thousands of verified, open-source programs that collectively establish tight upper bounds on the Kolmogorov complexity of each task. In this paper, we offer a comprehensive retrospective of the event, including an overview of the contest format, a survey of approaches taken by top teams, and a discussion of potential implications for the future design of intelligent agents.

items.title: The arc of uncertainty across clinicians’ interactions with AI
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used in various clinical settings to support clinical reasoning and decision-making. Although they have demonstrated strong performance on medical knowledge and reasoning tasks, and early studies suggest potential to reduce medical errors, emerging evidence also highlights important safety concerns, including clinically significant management errors in outputs that may not be readily apparent to users. How these tools can be integrated into clinical practice to consistently lead to improved patient outcomes remains an open question. AI-assisted reasoning unfolds across a sequence of decisions: whether to use AI for the clinical question, how to engage with the tool, how to interpret its output, and whether to act. Each stage in this sequence introduces distinct risks, including inappropriate tool selection, incomplete or biased inputs, overconfidence in fluent responses, and failure to recognize error or appreciate nuance. These risks are further shaped by the same clinician factors that generally affect clinical reasoning such as experience, workload, and uncertainty management. Viewing the AI-clinician interaction as a process rather than a single moment highlights several key points of vulnerability but also opportunities for training. Ultimately, the safe use of AI may depend less on the quality of the model and more on the clinician’s ability to recognize when its outputs should be questioned, verified, or set aside.

items.title: The Cognitive Offloading Dilemma: Exploring How Generative AI Dependency Shapes Students’ Independent Thinking, Cognitive Confidence, and Intellectual Autonomy
items.abstract: A polished assignment can conceal who chose the method, weighed the evidence and reached the conclusion, which makes a student’s independent reasoning difficult to assess. Drawing on the metacognitive account of cognitive offloading and Social Cognitive Theory, this qualitative study examined how reliance on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) relates to independent thinking, cognitive confidence and intellectual autonomy. Semi-structured online interviews were conducted with 22 undergraduate and postgraduate students, aged 20 to 29, from universities in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, Pakistan, each describing a recent academic episode involving GenAI. Thematic analysis traced when students sought assistance, which decisions they delegated and how they later justified their choices, and produced six themes. Delegating study planning preserved autonomy when students kept control over content, whereas removing a familiar AI prompt exposed difficulty in selecting a method despite earlier success with calculations. Confidence also diverged from accuracy: one student withheld a sound answer without AI confirmation, while another trusted a diagnosis because AI agreed with it, although both had missed the same error. Comparing drafts, checking sources and answering peers’ questions helped students identify assumptions and give reasons for revision. The findings support assessment practices that distinguish producing an answer with assistance from being able to explain or defend it without assistance.

items.title: The Effect of Robot’s Verbal Communication in Mixed-Hearing Ability Teams
items.abstract: Although robots show great potential as teammates, most researchers have focused on settings with a narrow view of possible human abilities, focusing on users without disabilities. Considering that verbal communication is one of the most widely used modalities in Human–Robot Interaction, its implications for teams composed of hearing and hard-of-hearing users remain underexplored. We set out to investigate this research gap by conducting an empirical study (N=16) in which a Tagi robot plays a collaborative game with two human participants, one is deaf or hard-of-hearing, and the other is hearing. We manipulated the communication modalities employed by the robot, verbal or non-verbal, in a within-subjects design. Our results showed that the verbal robot (compared to the non-verbal) sparked more non-verbal behaviours among participants, and that despite hearing participants perceived the robot as more animate and fair, deaf and hard of hearing participants felt more excluded. Finally, broader implications for social robots in mixed-hearing ability groups are discussed.

items.title: The Effects of AI Readiness, HRM Practices, and Continuous Learning Culture on HR Analytics Capability in Public Service Organizations
items.abstract: The study aims to investigate the effect of AI Readiness, HRM Practices and Continuous Learning Culture to HR Analytics Capability in public sector enterprises in Indonesia. The research was conducted based on a quantitative approach and the survey technique. The research participants consisted of the workers of public sector organizations who have expertise in the use of digital information systems and management of personnel data. The data were collected using an online questionnaire through Google Forms. The questions used a five-point Likert scale. The sampling technique used purposive sampling. Multiple linear regression was used to explore HR Analytics Capability in relation to the three independent variables. The proposed study model indicates that AI Readiness, HRM Practices and Continuous Learning Culture are positively related to HR Analytics Capability. AI Readiness is expected to have the highest relative impact. Artificial intelligence preparation may enhance the organizational capacity to integrate, analyze and use personnel data. Quality information is available with good human resource management practices. Moreover, a culture of continuous learning promotes the enhancement of employees’ analytical skills, teamwork and flexibility. The report provides practical implications for public service companies in terms of the value of strengthening AI infrastructure, data quality, digital competences, human resource management practices and promoting a culture of continuous learning for achieving HR Analytics Capability.

items.title: THE EVOLUTION AND ETHICAL INTEGRATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MODERN EDUCATION: A FRAMEWORK FOR PERSONALIZED LEARNING AND INSTITUTIONAL ACCOUNTABILITY
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has come a long way from its early theoretical days in the mid -1950s to become an advanced, data-based system that can learn from experience and execute jobs automatically. At present times, AI acts as a game-changer in education by making possible customized educational experiences based on the use of machine learning frameworks that provide individual guidance to every student, taking into account their speed, behaviour, preferences, and accomplishments. The change of this technological nature means that the role of a teacher must be shifted to the one who should now only provide guidance and help in, additionally, overseeing the machines. Beyond classrooms, AI adoption is a priority for national policies. For instance, India’s National Education Policy 2020 requires the teaching of AI and computational thinking in schools. The curriculum is set to start from Grade 3 in the academic year 2026-27. However, the rise of AI may create some challenges in terms of socio-economics. While AIED researchers are usually driven by the goals of enhancing learning results, the experience from other fields of AI indicates that good intentions do not guarantee ethical use of the technology. Important issues such as data ownership, algorithm bias, transparency, and student agency still remain unresolved. There is a necessity of collaborative endeavours in the creation of a community-wide framework in addressing the difference between "doing ethical things" and "doing things ethically. The PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework is a prominent method for ensuring transparency and repeatability in systematic reviews and can be used in the mapping of the enormous literature in this evolving sphere, while the mentioned resources mainly rely on expert surveys of leading scientists to define the major shortcomings.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON THE EFFECTIVENESS OF TEACHING ACTIVITY
items.abstract: This article examines how artificial intelligence affects teaching effectiveness in three areas: lesson preparation, instructional support during learning, and students’ independent performance. A comparative analysis of five international studies considers what each AI tool was designed to do, how it was used, and which outcomes were measured. In a school-based trial, teachers given access to ChatGPT and a practical guide spent less time preparing science lessons and materials. In mathematics tutoring, real-time AI support helped tutors ask more probing questions, and their students were more likely to master the topics covered. Research on AI tutoring also highlights the importance of assessing what students can do independently. In one mathematics experiment, unrestricted AI assistance improved performance during practice, but students scored lower than the control group when they later worked without the tool. An AI tutor that offered teacher-designed hints mitigated this effect. For pedagogical universities in Uzbekistan, the analysis identifies three priorities for preparing future teachers: reviewing AI-generated teaching materials, using AI to support questioning and feedback, and assessing what students can do without AI assistance.

items.title: The impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on employee green well-being: The mediating role of employee engagement in Vietnamese enterprises
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into workplaces is transforming not only how employees perform their tasks but also how they experience work. However, the implications of this transformation for sustainable development remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding whether AI-enabled workplaces can support employees’ long-term well-being and resilience. Addressing this gap, this study examines how positive attitudes toward Generative AI (POS_ATT) and responsible AI signals (RAIS) contribute to multidimensional Green Well-being through employee engagement (ENG). Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Signaling Theory, and the Job Demands–Resources theory, Green Well-being is conceptualized as a sustainable state encompassing emotional (GEW), cognitive (GCW), and social well-being (GSW). A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 342 knowledge workers employed by Vietnamese organizations using Generative AI. Participants were recruited using convenience and snowball sampling. The proposed model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results show that both POS_ATT (β = 0.312, p < 0.001) and RAIS (β = 0.287, p < 0.001) are positively associated with employee engagement. ENG, in turn, is positively associated with all three dimensions of Green Well-being, with the strongest relationship observed for emotional well-being (β = 0.441), followed by cognitive (β = 0.418) and social well-being (β = 0.397), all at p < 0.001. Moreover, ENG fully mediates the relationships between POS_ATT and RAIS and the three Green Well-being dimensions. These findings broaden understanding of sustainable development in AI-enabled workplaces by showing that the potential human benefits of Generative AI are not associated solely with technology adoption. Rather, favorable employee perceptions and responsible implementation need to be translated into meaningful work engagement before they are associated with sustainable well-being outcomes. The study therefore identifies responsible AI, employee engagement, and multidimensional well-being as interconnected elements of a human-centered approach to sustainable digital transformation. Practically, organizations should complement investments in AI capabilities with transparent, explainable, and fair AI governance and engagement-oriented work design to preserve and develop human resources during digital transformation. Because the cross-sectional design captures relationships at a single point in time, the findings establish associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and cross-national research is therefore needed to examine whether these relationships persist over time and contribute to long-term employee and organizational resilience. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; responsible AI; employee engagement; Green Well-being; sustainable development; sustainable digital transformation.

items.title: The Invisible Value of Visible Algorithms: AI Decision Transparency and Knowledge Sharing
items.abstract: AI decision transparency can help employees understand algorithmic decisions, yet the psychological mechanisms through which such transparency promotes knowledge-sharing behavior remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory, this study examines the mediating roles of self-determination and AI self-efficacy, as well as the moderating role of perceived organizational support. Using three-wave survey data from 315 knowledge workers in China, we tested a moderated parallel mediation model through multiple regression analysis and bootstrapping with 5000 resamples. The findings indicate that AI decision transparency is positively associated with both psychological resources, which, in turn, are positively related to knowledge-sharing behavior through distinct autonomy-related and capability belief pathways. Perceived organizational support further strengthens these relationships, with significant moderated mediation effects observed for both pathways. By elucidating how external informational resources are linked to resource reinvestment behavior through distinct psychological resources, this study extends the application of COR theory to AI-enabled workplaces and highlights the importance of supportive organizational environments in realizing the potential knowledge-sharing benefits of AI transparency.

items.abstract: This research on study of students' motivation learning in Law using a process approach of 1st year in Faculty of Food Science, Savannakhet University, during the 2024-2025 academic year. Including 31 participants, 10 females (representing majors in Agribusiness and Marketing, Food Processing Technology, and Rural Development and Business Promotion) were selected via purposive sampling. The research instruments included lesson plans, pre-tests and post-tests, and a behavioral observation scale covering five dimensions: collaborative planning in group work, mutual assistance among members, enthusiasm and accuracy in data research, group and individual responsibility, and clarity and engagement in presentations. The research followed a one-group pre-test/post-test experimental design. Statistical analysis was conducted using percentages (%), mean (), standard deviation (S.D.), and the Dependent Sample t-test. The findings indicate that the learning outcomes for the Law course using the process approach method were significantly higher in the post-test than the pre-test, with a post-test mean score of () = 7.77 (S.D = 1.54) at a statistical significance level of 0.01. Behavioral observations revealed that students actively participated in activities, demonstrated high responsibility in group tasks, and supported one another. Students showed increased interest and enthusiasm due to the opportunities for self-directed thinking. Regarding attitudes toward the process approach teaching method, the evaluation score was 3.92, categorized at a "Good" level. This method emphasizes teamwork, review and exchange, which aids students in achieving accurate long-term retention. Furthermore, the study on student motivation revealed that both intrinsic and extrinsic motivations were present; however, intrinsic motivation was more dominant, with an overall mean of 4.84 compared to 3.55 for extrinsic motivation. In conclusion, intrinsic motivation is the exceptional for students in Faculty of Food Science, Savannakhet University.

items.title: THE TRILLION-DOLLAR PROOF INDUSTRY: WHY AI COMPANIES WEAPONIZE THE MILLENNIUM PROBLEMS
items.abstract: Commercial Weaponization of Prize Problems: Artificial intelligence companies have transformed the one-million-dollar Clay Millennium Prize Problems into multi-trillion-dollar marketing vehicles, using binary formal proofs to project absolute reliability ahead of enterprise sales cycles and initial public offerings. Mathematical Vaudeville: Corporate publicity campaigns repackage physically sterile stunts—such as contrived blow-up constructions in idealized three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations—and choreographed preprints on Yang-Mills theory and the Riemann Hypothesis as historic breakthroughs, despite offering no practical value for real fluid turbulence or engineering. Closed Formal Cages vs. Brute-Force Search: AI laboratories target Millennium problems because they are finite games with fixed axioms, bounded inference rules, and automated pass/fail verification signals, making them tractable via massive parallel tree search and reinforcement learning. The Chasm with Fundamental Physics: Unlike solving a pre-stated puzzle inside an unchanging logical labyrinth, discovering new laws of nature requires dismantling flawed axioms, interpreting physical anomalies, and creating new mathematical structures anchored in conservation laws and experimental reality. Distortion of Scientific Priorities: Funneling capital and prestige toward mechanical benchmark clearance sidelines slow, foundational inquiry and confuses automated verification with genuine physical discovery.

items.title: UNDERGRADUATE EFL LEARNERS' PERCEPTIONS OF VERIFICATION AND DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS IN AI-ASSISTED WRITING ASSESSMENT
items.abstract: Universities increasingly ask students to verify AI-generated content and to reveal AI help, but there is little knowledge of how EFL students experience these demands. This explanatory sequential mixed methods study investigated a convenience sample of 60 undergraduate EFL students at a Pakistani university for perceived utility, verification confidence, effort, honesty and willingness to reveal, then interviewed ten students. Most students (71.7%) agreed that verification helped them to take responsibility for accuracy but only 45.0% agreed that disclosure made writing more transparent, and that the willingness to make it public was the lowest for heavily revised text (42.4%). The willingness to disclose was the most associated with perceived fairness (ρ = .58). The perceived confidence in effort and verification was higher among frequent AI users and advanced students and only 45.0% of students reported receiving guidance on disclosure. Interview notes pointed to concerns about the quality and currency of AI-generated writing, fear about reduced brands as AI usage is announced, and a need for institutional guidance. Clear rules, practical disclosure examples, and training in checking references may make these demands fairer. Findings are exploratory, self-reported and context-specific, and two scales were in a low degree of reliability. Keywords: generative AI; EFL writing; AI disclosure; verification; academic integrity; writing assessment; student perceptions; Pakistan

items.title: Using AI to Improve Interpersonal Skills in Undergraduate Teams: A Focused Review and Classroom Exercise
items.abstract: An undergraduate can rehearse raising a missed deadline with a chatbot and still struggle when a teammate gives an unexpected explanation. This focused narrative review examines nine empirical studies according to the role of artificial intelligence (AI), the outcome assessed, and whether AI was available during assessment. The evidence most directly relevant to undergraduate team conflict documents strategies used during chatbot rehearsal and students’ reported confidence after instruction and practice. Studies in adjacent settings illustrate how to assess unaided performance with a human partner. Controlled studies in clinical settings show mixed results for the added benefit of AI practice. The reviewed evidence leaves open whether undergraduate students use the targeted behaviors in ordinary team interactions after AI rehearsal. A proposed classroom exercise combines AI rehearsal, behavior-based feedback, and unaided peer conversations. It distinguishes immediate application to a new scenario, delayed retention, and observation in actual teamwork. A proposed research design compares AI rehearsal with an equivalent amount of peer rehearsal.

items.title: When Humanlike AI Feels Wrong: Perceived Eeriness and Trust in AI-Mediated Brand Communication — A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Background: This review examines when humanlike artificial intelligence (AI) becomes unsettling and how uncanny appraisal relates to consumer trust in AI-mediated brand communication. It integrates the trust-building logic of anthropomorphism with evidence of unfavorable trust-related evaluations under uncanny conditions. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 and SPAR-4-SLR principles, a Scopus search identified 7,665 records. After duplicate, document-type, and title/abstract screening, 18 journal articles were retained, verified in full text, and coded by AI form, appraisal mechanism, trust object, boundary condition, outcome, and evidence directness. Additional theoretical sources were used for conceptual anchoring but were not added to the systematic evidence corpus. Results: Five studies provide direct uncanny-appraisal evidence, six proximal-appraisal evidence, and seven contextual anthropomorphism–trust evidence. Direct studies associate unfavorable uncanny appraisal with lower trust-related evaluation, using distinct measures of affect, trust, and source trustworthiness. Human-likeness is not inherently harmful: social cues can support trust when aligned with competence, empathy, usefulness, transparency, and task demands. Conclusion: The review develops the Eeriness-Trust Calibration Framework (ETCF), separating design cues from consumer appraisals, positive and negative trust routes, and multiple trust objects. It reframes AI humanization as a cue-capability-context calibration problem and identifies cross-object trust transfer to organizations and brands as a key unresolved marketing mechanism. Brands should optimize coherence rather than maximize realism, pretest eeriness and authenticity together, and monitor trust separately at agent, content, provider, and brand levels.

items.title: When machines imagine. A pedagogy of artificial imagination for educational engagement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence intervenes in the domain of imagination by making images, narratives, and possible worlds immediately available, often preceding the learner’s own exploration and elaboration. Drawing on theoretical analysis and empirical evidence, this paper brings Munari’s distinction among fantasy, invention, creativity, and imagination into dialogue with sociocultural approaches and theories of material engagement. It conceptualises artificial imagination as a transformation of the symbolic and material environment in which human imaginative activity unfolds, without attributing imagination, in the human sense, to AI systems. Techno-material plasticity describes the twofold influence of technological devices: they shape the conditions of generation and enable subsequent transformations of generated forms. Research on learning, engagement, and creativity indicates educational potential alongside risks of fixation, homogenisation, and delegation. On this basis, the paper outlines a pedagogy of engagement centred on learners’ interpretive agency: autonomous elaboration before generation, critical examination of errors and impossibilities, manipulation and recomposition of outputs, and reflective documentation of processes. The educational value of generation depends on treating outputs as material for further elaboration while preserving the time required for experience, judgement, and learner authorship.

items.title: Workplace ergonomics, self-reported musculoskeletal symptoms and sedentary behaviour among desk-based office employees in Islamabad, Pakistan: a cross-sectional survey of employees and human resources officers with an embedded qualitative component
items.abstract: Poor workplace ergonomics is a growing yet under-investigated occupational health concern in Pakistan’s expanding corporate sector. This study estimated the prevalence of self-reported musculoskeletal symptoms; described perceived workplace ergonomic conditions and sedentary behaviour among desk-based employees in Islamabad; examined their correlates; and documented organisational ergonomic practices as reported by human resources (HR) officers. A cross-sectional survey with an embedded qualitative (free-text) component was conducted in Islamabad between 2024 and 2025 among a purposive sample of 251 respondents: 179 desk-based office employees and 72 HR officers. Employees and HR officers were recruited independently and could not be linked to one another at the organisational level, so the two strands are reported as complementary perspectives and never as a paired organisational comparison. Two distinct instruments were used. The employee instrument, informed by the item content of the Cornell Musculoskeletal Discomfort Questionnaire (CMDQ) and the Rapid Office Strain Assessment (ROSA) checklist, captured self-reported symptoms, workstation characteristics and sedentary patterns; neither tool was administered as a scored assessment. The HR instrument captured organisation-level ergonomic policy and practice. The two instruments shared no items in common, so the two groups are reported separately and not pooled. Qualitative data came from open-ended items embedded in the employee survey; we conducted no in-depth interviews. Analyses in SPSS version 21 comprised frequencies with 95% confidence intervals, chi-square tests and multivariable logistic regression. We conducted inductive thematic analysis of open-ended responses, integrating themes through a joint display. Associations are cross-sectional and are reported as adjusted odds ratios; they describe associations, not prediction or causation. Among the 179 employees, 124 (69.3%) had never received ergonomic training, although 156 (87.2%) believed ergonomic improvement would reduce workplace fatigue. An adjustable chair supporting the back was available to 106 (59.2%) and a screen at eye level to 120 (67.0%). At least one musculoskeletal symptom was reported by 127 (70.9%, 95% CI 64.3–77.6), and 102 (57.0%) reported symptoms at two or more body sites. Back pain was the most prevalent single symptom (100, 55.9%), followed by shoulder discomfort (98, 54.7%), eye strain or headaches (92, 51.4%), neck discomfort (90, 50.3%) and wrist pain (70, 39.1%). Persistent pain developing over time was reported by 84 (46.9%), and 62 (34.6%) had sought medical treatment. Sixty-eight employees (38.0%) sat for seven hours or more daily, and 53 (29.6%) rarely took movement breaks. A screen positioned at eye level was independently associated with lower odds of neck discomfort (adjusted OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.15–0.70), shoulder discomfort (0.33, 95% CI 0.15–0.73), and back pain (0.32, 95% CI 0.15–0.69). Female employees reported substantially higher symptom prevalence than male employees at every site (any symptom 86.6% versus 61.6%; adjusted OR for male sex 0.22, 95% CI 0.09–0.53). Among HR officers, 44 (61.1%) reported a formal ergonomics policy; only 24 (33.3%) reported that their organisation provided ergonomic training; 25 (34.7%) tracked discomfort reports; and 44 (61.1%) allocated under 5% of the budget to ergonomic improvements. Thematic analysis identified five organisational barriers: budgetary constraints, managerial knowledge gaps, organisational inertia, spatial limitations and reluctance to raise complaints. Self-reported musculoskeletal symptoms were common among desk-based employees in this Islamabad sample, and basic ergonomic provisions and training were frequently absent. Screen height was the workstation characteristic most consistently associated with symptoms, and female employees carried a markedly higher symptom burden. HR officers commonly reported formal ergonomic policies, while employees commonly reported a lack of training and monitoring; because the two respondent groups were not linked at the organisational level, these are complementary perspectives on ergonomic provision and do not demonstrate organisation-level discordance. Workstation review, ergonomic training and accessible reporting channels are plausible low-cost priorities; prospective and intervention studies are required to establish causation and effectiveness.

items.title: WORKPLACE WELLBEING AND MENTAL HEALTH IN SUSTAINABLE HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT
items.abstract: The mental health of employees can be affected by factors including workload, supervision, job security, and availability of support. Organisations often focus on offering support such as counselling, awareness activities and tools to help individuals. This conceptual paper explores how sustainable HRM can be used to link services to changes in working conditions. It draws together guidance from occupational health, sustainable HRM literature and theories around job demands, resources, motivation and psychological safety. This has led to the development of the Sustainable Well-being HRM model. The model includes six areas of practice; psychosocial risk management, job enrichment, inclusive leadership, mental health awareness and support, fair flexibility and adjustment, and accountability. A prevention hierarchy, matrix of practice and implementation plan demonstrate how each of these can be embedded into current HR practices. This paper also develops propositions for future research. This paper contributes to the field by bringing together existing concepts into a practical model. However, the model has not been verified therefore the relationships should be viewed as propositions. The analysis suggests that employers should consider the impacts of changes to working conditions when implementing wellbeing initiatives. Whilst protecting mental health may not always be easy to show clear financial gains it is an ethical duty. items.title: Zero-Trust Formal Methods: AI Agents Build Verified Checkers for Untrusted Solvers
items.abstract: AI coding agents now generate code faster than humans can review it. Security analyses rely on solver answers such as "unsatisfiable" (for example, no attack path exists) or "optimal." Unlike satisfying models, they cannot be checked by looking at them. Formal verification moves trust from code to specifications, but verifiers still place large SAT, SMT, and answer-set solvers, and the translation into solver queries, in their trusted computing base, and these have had soundness bugs. Unlike agent-based pipelines that trust their verifier and solver, our farm trusts no component by default: neither the AI agents, which might make mistakes or game their objectives, nor the solvers. A solver answer counts only if a verified checker accepts its certificate. Every theory, proof, and line of code is generated by AI. For each component, agents first create an Isabelle/HOL theory with a specification, a soundness proof, and a reference checker made by code generation, then a fast Rust implementation, verified with Verus against a specification that mirrors the Isabelle definitions line by line. Specifications are frozen after independent review and cannot be changed by the implementing agents. A trust manifest lists what is still trusted. We built trust chains for SAT (verified LRAT checking); SMT, with certificates from an extended z3 and verified bit-blasting for bit-vectors and floating point; answer-set programming, with native certificates from clingo, including weight rules and optimality; and, closing the loop, Verus's final verification-condition step, by translation validation. All 3,726 SMT queries from 20 crates are certified and validated, and 15,662 answer-set proofs are accepted by both the Isabelle and the Verus checker. We found soundness defects in three proof checkers, including drat-trim, and in five solvers, including clasp and z3, which report wrong unsatisfiability.

items.title: 4328-GRP ProgCT: Cultivating Computational Thinking with Pedagogy-Grounded AI Agents
items.abstract: Computational Thinking (CT) develops critical thinking and problem-solving skills in learners systematically. Modern AI tutors can help learners solve problems effectively; however, they generate direct answers and mostly fail to integrate the pedagogical principles focused on CT components to improve students’ problem-solving skills. This failure raises concern in the development of CT skills for early learners. Our project, ProgCT is a pedagogy-grounded multi-agent tutor that helps learners develop computational problem-solving abilities through CT practices. As learners work through each problem, the agents (i) assess the CT skills learners demonstrate, (ii) analyze learners’ cognitive engagement, and (iii) guide learners through the relevant CT steps with Socratic hints without revealing the solution. In a pretest post-test study on Python programming concepts involving seven learners (n=7), the mean score of the Algorithmic Thinking Test for Adults (ATTA) rose from 64.8% to 77.6%, and self-assessed confidence on the Hi-ACT test increased in all six CT components – abstraction, decomposition, pattern recognition, algorithm design, evaluation and generalization. The system’s built-in progress evaluation module also recorded increases in participants’ CT ownership and cognitive engagement on later exercises compared with earlier exercises of the same difficulty.

items.title: A Digital Stress Resilience Model for Sustainable Performance and Responsible Organizations
items.abstract: The rapid Digitalization of organizational work, accelerated by Artificial Intelligence, hybrid work, ubiquitous connectivity, and continuous information exchange, has created unprece dented opportunities for productivity. Simultaneously the issues of intensifying digital overload, cognitive fatigue, work interruptions, technostress, and emotional exhaustion have been non-trivial challenges for organizations. Existing organizational stress-management approaches predominantly emphasize individual coping or post-stress interventions and provide limited integration of real-time Digital Stress detection, adaptive regulation, responsible technology governance, and sustainable productivity. Addressing the above challenges and the research gap, we propose a Digital Stress Resilience Model grounded in Sustainable Positive Computing, Self-awareness, Affective Computing, Organizational Psychology, and Responsible Artificial intelligence. Our proposed model conceptualizes Digital Stress Management as a continuous socio-technical process comprising five interconnected capabilities such as Digital Stress Perception, Cognitive-Emotional Intelligence, Adaptive Stress Regulation, Responsible Digital Governance, and Resilience-Oriented Productivity Management. The model provides a conceptual roadmap for transforming organizations from reactive stress-management environments into proactive, self-aware, resilient, responsible, and productive digital workplaces. A mixed-method research design is proposed for subsequent empirical validation using digital workload, cognitive load, emotional regulation, resilience, responsible technology use, employee engagement, and sustainable productivity indicators.
